The compiler can store the size anywhere it sees fit, it is usually going to be in the stack or in some register just like a variable. Here is an example: 
 #include <stddef.h>

size_t g();

void f()
{
 volatile char arr1[g()];
 for (size_t i = 0; i < sizeof(arr1); ++i)
 arr1[i] = 0;
}
 
 GCC compiles the code above to this x64 code: 
 f:
 push rbp
 xor eax, eax
 mov rbp, rsp
 call g
 lea rdx, [rax+15]
 and rdx, -16
 sub rsp, rdx
 test rax, rax
 je .L1
 mov rcx, rsp
 xor edx, edx
 test al, 1
 je .L3
 mov BYTE PTR [rsp], 0
 mov edx, 1
 cmp rax, 1
 je .L1
.L3:
 mov BYTE PTR [rcx+rdx], 0
 mov BYTE PTR [rcx+1+rdx], 0
 add rdx, 2
 cmp rax, rdx
 jne .L3
.L1:
 leave
 ret
 
 This C code creates a VLA using the result of calling a function g defined elsewhere. Since in x64 Linux functions return integers in rax , the compiler uses the value in rax to calculate a new size for the stack frame. Then it uses rax in the loop condition because the array’s size was already there anyway: 
 add rdx, 2
cmp rax, rdx
jne .L3
 
 So in this case the array’s size stays always in rax . 
 In general, if the array size is calculated at runtime the compiler can simply reuse the same register where the final calculation is. It might also move it to the stack if it decides to use the register for something else. So in the generated machine code the size of a VLA behaves just like a variable. 
 That being said, the above Assembly code shows how you don’t need the size of the array to undo the new stack frame. The stack frame is created by pushing the base pointer rbp onto the stack, moving the value in the stack pointer rsp to rbp and then decrementing rsp . When returning we simply move the value in rbp back to rsp , making rsp point to the top of the stack where the previous value of rbp was, then we pop the value from the top of the stack back into rbp . This is what the leave instruction does.

TLDR for those who came here looking for clues when facing Bochs' log like fetch_raw_descriptor: GDT: index (ff57) 1fea > limit (2f) : 
 Start Bochs with the debugger enabled, execute show int & show dbg_all in the Bochs debugger CLI, and then run your image. This would make Bochs to log all interrupts/exceptions; if this error occurred during interrupt handling, you'll get some more clues into what was happening. 
 
 Now, to the question.
First let's see the logs. 
 19849108391e[CPU0 ] fetch_raw_descriptor: GDT: index (ff57) 1fea > limit (2f)
19849108391e[CPU0 ] interrupt(): gate descriptor is not valid sys seg (vector=0x08)
 
 Vector 0x08 is a double fault vector. So presumably there was some exception, and the attempt to process it resulted in a double fault. Moreover, the attempt to process a double fault
also resulted in a fault, presumably because the trap segments value in IDT was not a valid system segment. Something is wrong in your IDT; and also there was that first exception, so something is wrong there too. 
 19849108391i[CPU0 ] | EAX=00100023...
19849108391i[CPU0 ] | ESP=00800000...
19849108391i[CPU0 ] | SEG sltr(index|ti|rpl) base limit G D
19849108391i[CPU0 ] | CS:001b( 0003| 0| 3) 00000000 ffffffff 1 1
19849108391i[CPU0 ] | DS:0023( 0004| 0| 3) 00000000 ffffffff 1 1
19849108391i[CPU0 ] | SS:0023( 0004| 0| 3) 00000000 ffffffff 1 1
19849108391i[CPU0 ] | EIP=00100023 (00100023)
19849108391i[CPU0 ] | CR2=0x00100023
19849108391i[CPU0 ] 0x0000000000100023>> or byte ptr ds:[esi-117], ah : 08668B
 
 Ok, so the exception happens upon jump to User mode. CS is 0x1B as expected, and the rest of the segments are 0x23 as expected. ESP is 0x800000 as expected. It seems the cross-privilege level iret did its job. The segment shadow contents looks fine as well. 
 EIP looks wrong however. It points into the kernel, somewhere in the middle of an instruction. CR2 is the same as EIP which suggests the initial exception was a paging exception; CPU couldn't read the code instruction (which is expected I guess if the kernel pages are set as system). EAX is the same as EIP (and it holds the initial EIP value in enter_user_mode , so probably the very first instruction faulted). 
 19849108391e[CPU0 ] exception(): 3rd (13) exception with no resolution, shutdown status is 00h, resetting
 
 This is the triple-fault reset, because a double-fault could not be processed. 
 Ok, so 1) exception handling doesn't work, and it should(?) and 2) a bad EIP. 
 That 0x23 in the end of EIP is highly suspect, because it matches the data segment value. Surely enough, enter_user_mode is buggy: 
 00100b10 <enter_user_mode>:
 100b10: fa cli
 100b11: 8b 44 24 04 mov 0x4(%esp),%eax
 100b15: 66 b8 23 00 mov $0x23,%ax
 
 EIP value gets loaded into eax , but then ax is also loaded with 0x23 which destroys half of the value. Fix is trivial: simply use different registers; e.g. use 'dx' for the selector value. 
 With that fixed, we get 
 19960859176i[CPU0 ] | EIP=00108000 (00108000)
19960859176i[CPU0 ] | CR2=0x00108000
19960859176i[CPU0 ] 0x0000000000108000>> mov eax, 0xdeadbeef : B8EFBEADDE
 
 Ok, so now it faults at the actual usermode start. Why does it do that? Well, because it’s still a system-mode page. There is nothing in your code to prepare the actual user-mode region of virtual addresses. From the book (para 11.2): 
 
 There are a few things every user mode process needs:
Page frames for code, data and stack. At the moment it suffices to allocate one page frame for the stack and enough page frames to fit the program’s code. Don’t worry about setting up a stack that can be grow and shrink at this point in time, focus on getting a basic implementation work first.
The binary from the GRUB module has to be copied to the page frames used for the programs code.
A page directory and page tables are needed to map the page frames described above into memory. At least two page tables are needed, because the code and data should be mapped in at 0x00000000 and increasing, and the stack should start just below the kernel, at 0xBFFFFFFB, growing towards lower addresses. The U/S flag has to be set to allow PL3 access. 
 
 None of that has been done. There isn’t any stack space allocated, and there aren’t any user-mode pages to hold the user-space code. This fault is expected; the kernel just isn't ready to run userspace. 
 Ok, with that figured out, let's return to the IDT handling. Looking at interrupts_install_idt , it is immediately obvious that it could use some love. At least the internal exceptions handlers should be all filled up (also note exception 7 is not error-code bearing; the list of such exceptions is provided in the book). It would be a good idea to add some handling of the exceptions also; one common approach is to log an exception, CPU, state, etc. Well, see the Bochs log for an example. Your code could do something similar. 
 I have to say the book has dropped the ball here. This is a tricky subject, and the book gives two rough examples of C side (paragraph 6.3) and assembly side (paragraph 6.4) of interrupt handler, but they are not compatible with each other! interrupt_handler has to be called according to its declaration (or vice versa); kudos to you for fixing that (I am not sure if struct ordering is correct though). 
 All that said, the code does look fine at first glance. It should've been a page fault, which should've been handled at least somehow. Moreover, Bochs debugger can show IDT contents, and it's fine; the segment values are correct. Let's switch Bochs' debugging logs on and see what's happening in more details ("show int", "show dbg_all" in the Bochs debugger CLI): 
 CPU 0: Exception 0x0e - (#PF) page fault occurred (error_code=0x0005)
CPU 0: Interrupt 0x0e occurred (error_code=0x0005)
07358149912e[CPU0 ] fetch_raw_descriptor: GDT: index (ff57) 1fea > limit (2f)
CPU 0: Exception 0x0a - (#TS) invalid TSS occurred (error_code=0xff51)
CPU 0: Exception 0x08 - (#DF) double fault occurred (error_code=0x0000)

That involves switching the stack, and switching the stack needs TSS (so the CPU has a place to store ring 3 SS/ESP and load ring 0 SS/ESP). There isn’t any TSS set in the code, and therefore any exceptions in ring 3 would result in a crash. Well, the book hints at such problems in paragraph 11.3:

<iostream> was originally modeled after the legacy C printf API lacking support for binary format. It was meant to make a safe replacement for variadic functions. 
 It wasn't until C++14 that the 0b prefix was adopted into C++ as the binary literal value indicator, and by that time, the critical design flaws of <iostream> were well-known. Besides that the C++11 adoption of variadic templates had already started the quest for simpler interfaces.
Today <iostream> is maintained as legacy burden. 
 The output is now carried out using C++23 header <print> with std::print , and std::println handling standard output as well as formatted file output to std::ostream , std::ofstream , and the C API std::FILE * . The new std::formatter adds support for binary through b format argument. 
 On a C++20 setup <format> gives std::format — using same std::formatter — as the replacement for sprintf . So combination of std::puts , or std::fputs with std::format and std::string::c_str can temporarily fill in the place of <print> . 
 Otherwise the refrence implementation of <format> and <print> is the {fmt} library — compatible with C++17 . 
 All in all, <iostream> is only being used for istream input, in modern code. If {scanlib} hits the maturity level of {fmt} , or a better implementation of C++ regexp emerges, we can finally totally retire <iostream> as deprecated. So, short answer to original question is that <iostream> is not worth more investment.

One major reason for not looking for your proposed optimization is that it's super niche (noreturn functions are rare), and doesn't save instructions. Also, it would conflict with keeping any of your own local vars in your incoming shadow space , and many functions have local vars. 
 (Compiler devs have to balance the value of an optimization against the amount of compile time it takes to look for it, and the maintenance / testing burden of the compiler code that looks for it. Not just the development time of a new feature, but ongoing cost in slower builds, larger source code, and something that could potentially break and lead to miscompiled programs when other parts of the compiler internals are being reworked.) 
 It only helps with speed by reusing a cache line of stack space that's already hot... once in the lifetime of a thread. Sure you could construct a corner case where this avoids a page fault to grow the stack, but very often the saving would be totally trivial. 
 Often a tailcall is possible (like jmp exit ) and does as good a job at giving our shadow space to a callee. ( exit may be marked as special to have GCC not tailcall it, so debuggers can see where it was called from. abort() is marked that way, so the backtrace it generates doesn't omit its actual caller. Or maybe your GCC just chooses to use call instead of add $40, %rsp / jmp exit since it already has the stack set up for a call. And that's fine since the stack memory below RSP is probably already hot in cache since we just make another call.) 
 As far as I can tell, GCC doesn't seem to have any special attributes other than noreturn for functions like abort : https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Common-Function-Attributes.html#index-noreturn-function-attribute says - In order to preserve backtraces, GCC will never turn calls to noreturn functions into tail calls. So doing other things that break backtraces should also be avoided for callers of noreturn functions. This proposed optimization would still allow seeing which function called abort , but not further up the call stack: what you're doing is almost like a tailcall, but we overwrite our incoming return address with a return address into this function. So instead of skipping ourselves in the call-chain, we break the chain, losing any reference to our parent function. 
(Semi-related: Why does the C compiler save registers in a noreturn function? ) 
 
 Allocating local variables (other than incoming register args) into shadow space is something MSVC does (but not GCC or Clang) , since that's a generally useful optimization and it can save instructions in leaf functions, or ones that exit via tailcall, if they never have to move RSP at all. 
( Godbolt - MSVC does it for volatile int a,b; , volatile long long a,b (16 bytes), or volatile int arr[2] , but not for volatile int arr[4]; (16 bytes)) 
 e.g. void foo(){ volatile long long a=1; } compiles with MSVC to mov QWORD PTR a$[rsp], 1 / ret , where a$ is defined as a$ = 8 in its asm listing. So this is the first slot of shadow space. 
 
 Saving stack space isn't totally irrelevant; the same compilers we use for user-space are also used to compile kernel code. Kernel stacks are often 8K or 16K per thread, and not pageable . (Linux used to use 4K kernel stacks on 32-bit x86, but last I checked had raised it again for x86-64 from 8 to 16K. I don't know what Windows does.) 
 So it's good if compilers don't waste stack space gratuitously, but even 48 bytes is not much out of 8K if it only happens a couple times in a call chain. And noreturn functions are vanishingly rare in kernel code, especially higher up in the callstack where the space would be wasted across calls to many callees. (In kernel code, everything except ending a thread/task will return to user-space.) So this is probably irrelevant there. And as @chqrlie says, stack space is not a precious commodity in user-space on x86-64. Windows by default uses 1MiB user-space stacks, GNU/Linux 8MiB. 
 Most calling-conventions that GCC targets don't have shadows space, only a few like MIPS and Windows x64, so I'm not surprised it doesn't have optimization passes to look for ways to get the best use out of it. x86-64 is the most important target for MSVC, so it's a good thing it does better at using it for locals.

For historic reasons, the C standard allows NULL to be either an integer constant expression with value 0 or such an expression cast to void * . So NULL could be defined as 0 , which would have type int . It could even be 0L or 0ULL , which would have type long or unsigned long long , respectively, since these are also integer constant expressions with value 0. 
 Then the sentinel argument to your variadic function would have a type incompatible with the type of the strings you are passing. You could be passing int while the strings result in char * . When your function attempted to get the value of this sentinel argument using va_arg(…, char *) , the behavior would not be defined. 
 Additionally, note that your string arguments have type char * , not const char * . Again, this is for historic reasons; const was not originally in C, so string literals had type char * , and this was not changed when const was introduced. 
 So, to make your sentinel argument exactly match the strings, you should pass (char *) NULL . 
 Note 
 You can use (const char *) NULL even though const char * is not compatible with char * . This is because the C standard makes some exceptions in what types may be used with va_arg . C 2024 7.16.2.1 says it will work if:

Since you have tagged this as language-lawyer, then the answer is yes (the call is “legal”) for reasons you may not have expected. However, it is also yes for the reasons you were likely concerned about. 
 First, as you note, the prototype of strtol is long strtol(const char *restrict nptr, char **restrict endptr, int base); . In this, restrict has no effect. This is because qualifiers are effectively not part of a function type. C 1999 6.7.5.3 15 states that, for purposes of compatibility between function types, “each parameter declared with qualified type is taken as having the unqualified version of its declared type.” This means that long strtol(const char *restrict nptr, char **restrict endptr, int base); has the same effect as long strtol(const char *nptr, char **endptr, int base); ; the qualifiers are not part of the function type. 
 (The qualifiers do affect the code inside a function body, because there the qualifiers are part of the types of the parameters.) 
 Second, the definition of restrict imposes requirements on code that uses the identifiers (which would be code inside the implementation of the function), not on code that calls a function with qualifiers on its parameters. Therefore, the call is “legal” because it does not violate any requirements related to the qualifiers. 
 What you are probably wondering about is, if you call strtol as you have shown, would the code inside it satisfy the requirements on the qualifiers. From a language-lawyer perspective, we cannot know this because we cannot know what the code inside the function is. It might not even be C code, but, even if it is, there are ways to implement functions that work with overlapping memory through restricted pointers. Consider this: 
 void square(double * restrict result, double * restrict x)
{
 double t = *x;
 t = t*t;
 if (result == x)
 *x = t;
 else
 *result = t;
}
 
 This code writes the result to *result without violating the restrict requirements even if x and result point to the same place, because, if they do point to the same place, it uses *x to access that place and does not use *result . 
 However let’s suppose strtol was written naïvely, oblivious to the possibilities the pointers might point to overlapping memory, so that this strtol reads data through nptr (or expressions based on nptr and not endptr ) and writes the end pointer through endptr (or expressions based on endptr and not nptr ). Observe that all the objects in memory needed to read the string, those in the array induced by "1234" , are completely separate from the str object. The formal definition of restrict in C 1999 6.7.3.1 only imposes requirements on accesses to an object X that is modified during execution of the function (in this situation). They say that if X is accessed with an lvalue based on a restricted pointer, then every access to X will be based on that pointer. For the object str pointed to by endptr , our supposition is this is true: Every access to the object str is through an lvalue based on endptr . For the objects in "1234" , there is no modification to those objects, so the formal definition of restrict does not impose any requirements. 
 Therefore, even a naïve implementation of strtol satisfies the requirements of restrict .

This is the 'strong-ownership model', where the module strongly owns even exported symbols. Windows started with this, and GCC and Clang eventually moved to this due to some benefits seen with adding the module name to the mangling. 
 See: 
 https://github.com/itanium-cxx-abi/cxx-abi/pull/144 
 
 The strong-ownership model is implemented — the symbols of exported entities with named-module attachment are mangled with a module-name component. 
 
 https://gcc.gnu.org/git/?p=gcc.git;a=commit;h=73baba1ae1b8f3618c2d3b674117b8a462e0ca76 
 
 This implements a strong ownership model, so that exported entities
from named modules are mangled to include their module attachment.
This gives more informative linker diagnostics and better module
isolation. Weak ownership was hoped to allow backwards compatibility
with non-modular code, but in practice was very brittle, and C++20
added new semantics for linkage declarations that cover the needed
functionality. 
 
 https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/commit/ae4dce8659f313ca2034782583d31993212fa8bd 
 
 The hoped-for C++17 compatibility of weak ownership turns out to be

A since-deleted, putatively AI-generated answer (only users with sufficient reputation can view the link) actually provided good insights; let me provide a 100% human-generated perspective. 
 Your program works as intended ; the behaviors you observe are specific to [Windows] PowerShell. 
 There are two distinct, unrelated aspects to consider: 
 
 (a) Printing external program output to the console (terminal). 
 
 (b) Capturing such output in a file , using > , i.e. I/O redirection . 
 
 
 
 Re (a) 
 By design, both cmd.exe and PowerShell - unlike most POSIX-compatible shells such as Bash [0] - ensure that a newline is always printed following command output before re-printing their prompt string in interactive sessions - even if the external program output does not end in a newline, such as in your case. 
 Thus, a program printing, say, printf("foo"); produces the same display output as one emitting printf("foo\n"); : 
 
 Presumably, the design rationale is to ensure that the prompt string always prints at the start of a line, for visual consistency. 
There is no way to modify this behavior in PowerShell that I am aware of. [1] 
 
 Re (b) 
 While it is understandable to try to use an I/O redirection, > , to capture an external program's raw byte output , this does not work as intended in Windows PowerShell , the legacy, ships-with-Windows, Windows-only edition of PowerShell whose latest and final version is 5.1: 
 
 External-program output is invariably first decoded , based on the encoding stored in [Console]::OutputEncoding , ... 
 
 ... and then re-encoded on saving to the target file, using the default encoding of the Out-File cmdlet, of which > is a virtual alias, and that default encoding happens to be UTF-16 LE (in which ASCII-range characters such as h are represented as 2-byte sequences with the low-order byte representing the ASCII code point and the high-order byte being 0x0 , e.g. 68 00 for 'h' ), preceded by a BOM (the FF FE by sequence shown at the start of your Format-Hex output). 
 
 Additionally, the external-program output is decoded line by line , and each line is written to the target file with a trailing newline , using the platform-native newline format, which is CRLF on Windows ( \r\n , in printf terms) - whether or not the output's last line had a trailing newline. 
Thus, similarly to the to-console output, a program printing, say, printf("foo"); produces the same file content as one emitting printf("foo\n"); when redirected with > , the redirection operator 
 
 It is worth noting that even in PowerShell (Core) 7 (see below) the decoding behavior still applies with respect to further processing external-program output in memory , and the re-encoding behavior still applies when using explicit calls to file-saving cmdlets such as Out-File , though PowerShell 7 notably and commendably consistently defaults to BOM-less UTF-8 . [2] 
 
 The simplest way to ensure capturing of raw bytes from external programs in Windows PowerShell is to delegate to cmd.exe , whose > operator does just that: 
 # Windows PowerShell:
# Captures raw byte output from .\r.exe 
# Note: \ rather than / must be used for cmd.exe's sake.
cmd /c .\r.exe > output.txt
 
 
 
 By contrast, it does work as intended in PowerShell (Core) 7 , the modern, cross-platform, install-on-demand edition, in v7.4+ (older versions are now out of support), i.e. > captures raw byte output , the same way it does in cmd.exe and in POSIX-compatible shells such as Bash. 
 # PowerShell (Core) 7.4+:
 # Captures raw byte output from ./r.exe, both on Windows and Unix-like platforms.

The . operator and the -> operator aren't normal infix operators because the right hand part of either one is not a general expression (you aren't allowed to put anything in parentheses in there, unlike with regular infix operators). Rather, . <name> and -> <name> are postfix operators. Various operator precedence guides group . and -> together with infix operators, but this is not entirely correct. 
 (Language lawyer hat on) <name> is actually template_opt id-expression or, in C++26, also a splice-expression . The standard doesn't use the term "postfix operator", it calls expressions with . and -> at the top level "postfix expressions". (Language lawyer hat off) Still if we call postfix ++ a postfix operator, it's reasonable to call -> <name> the same way, because it is grouped together with postfix ++ and postfix -- and "indexing" (e.g., arrayName[5] ) and "function call". 
 Postfix operators can have precedence like infix operators, but one cannot assign precedence to . as if it were an infix operator. Rather, one must assign precedence to the whole . <name> thing. Otherwise, things like a.b+c could parse to a.(b+c) which wouldn't make any sense. 
 In C++, all postfix operators have strictly higher precedence than all infix operators. This is a reasonable decision shared by most if not all mainstream languages. 
While it is theoretically possible to have a.*b.c to parse as (a.*b).c , this parse would seem alien to C users which were the primary target audience of C++, and also would raise many further questions about a.*b++ and the like.

Since you're looking for an event-based solution (updating a metadata file on commit), a client-side Git hook is needed, specifically a pre-commit hook. 
 Note that Git on Windows comes with its own Bash shell and common Unix utilities, so a cross-platform solution is possible. 
 However, the following proof-of-concept for Windows delegates the work to Windows PowerShell , via its powershell.exe CLI. 
 
 It would even be easy to adapt the solution to Unix-like platforms (as an alternative to a pure Bash solution), given the availability of PowerShell (Core) 7 , the modern, cross-platform, install-on-demand edition: all it takes is to replace powershell.exe with pwsh in the code below. 
 
 Note that it is possible to make hook scripts run PowerShell code directly (rather than having to call the PowerShell CLI from a /bin/sh -interpreted script), though it requires a workaround: see the bottom section. 
 
 Either way, on Windows the assumption is that execution of PowerShell scripts has already been allowed on a given target machine (on Unix -like platforms this isn't necessary), such as with one-time configuration command 
 Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned -Force ; if not, you can enable script execution ad hoc by adding -ExecutionPolicy Bypass to the CLI calls, assuming that there aren't more restrictive GPO -based policies in place; see this answer for more information. 
 
 To also address the aspect of avoiding potential merge conflicts caused by meta.inf involving multiple repository clones, see VonC's helpful answer . 
 
 
 
 Setting up the pre-commmit hook: 
 
 From your repo's root directory, create file ./git/hooks/pre-commit , e.g., from PowerShell, with 
 New-Item ./git/hooks/pre-commit 
 
 Note: On Unix-like platforms you'd need to make this file executable , using 
 chmod +x ./git/hooks/pre-commit , but this isn't needed on Windows (where you'd have to invoke the command from Git Bash if you were to invoke it; however, on Windows all files default to having the executable ( x ) permission from Git Bash's perspective). 
 
 
 Place the following content in the file: 
 
 
 #!/bin/sh

# Among the files to be committed that reside in data/,
# determine the most recent last-modified timestamp
# and write it to 'meta.inf' and make the modified 'meta.inf' part of the commit.
powershell.exe -noprofile -c '
 git diff --cached --name-only data/ |
 Get-Item -Force -ErrorAction Ignore |
 Sort-Object -Property LastWriteTime |
 Select-Object -Last 1 |
 ForEach-Object {
 "[data]", "MostRecentLastModified=$($_.LastWriteTime.ToString("o"))" |
 Set-Content -ErrorAction Stop meta.inf
 git add meta.inf
 exit $LASTEXITCODE
 }
 exit 0
'
 
 Note: 
 
 git diff --cached --name-only data/ ensures that only files in the data/ subdirectory tree that are part of the ongoing commit are processed. 
 
 The above assumes that meta.inf is expected to conform to the Inf file format, using the self-chosen names [data] for the section and MostRecentLastModified for the key; adjust as needed. 
 
 The timestamp is using .NET's round-trip date-time string format; e.g. 
 2025-12-04T11:38:15.8774146-05:00 
 
 Example meta.inf content: 
 [data]
MostRecentLastModified=2025-12-04T11:38:15.8774146-05:00

I was thinking that GCC trunk is correct because it implements the post-C++20 rule to the letter. But I found an old CWG issue that contradicts with the new behavior (see below). I can't tell whether GCC is correct and the standard committee changed its mind, or GCC is incorrect and either the post-C++20 wording is defective or both I and GCC maintainer misread the new wording. 
 Before C++20, the specification says ( N4659 [basic.lookup.argdep]/3 ): 
 
 Let X be the lookup set produced by unqualified lookup and let Y be the lookup set produced by argument dependent lookup (defined as follows). If X contains 
 
 [...] 
 
 then Y is empty. Otherwise Y is the set of declarations found in the namespaces associated with the argument types as described below. 
 When considering an associated namespace, the lookup is the same as the lookup performed when the associated namespace is used as a qualifier except that: 
 
 [...] 
 Any namespace-scope friend functions or friend function templates declared in associated classes are visible within their respective namespaces even if they are not visible during an ordinary lookup. 
 [...] 
 
 
 Here X contains nothing, so Y consists of the declarations found in A 's associated namespace, which is the global namespace, which doesn't contain a declaration of f . The lookup finds nothing. 
 After C++20 (specifically, after the post-C++20 paper P1787R6 ), the specification says ( N4950 [basic.lookup.argdep]/4 ): 
 
 Argument-dependent lookup finds all declarations of functions and function templates that 
 
 are found by a search of any associated namespace, or 
 are declared as a friend ([class.friend]) of any class with a reachable definition in the set of associated entities, or 
 are exported, are attached to a named module M ([module.interface]), do not appear in the translation unit containing the point of the lookup, and have the same innermost enclosing non-inline namespace scope as a declaration of an associated entity attached to M ([basic.link]). 
 
 
 Note that in the second bullet, for functions that are declared as a friend, there's no restriction to the namespace. Hence it seems that ADL should find the declaration of ns::f . 
 I found GCC commit 8f6c9ebc7d7 which seems to be the commit that implements the new rule. It mentions that "in C++20 P1787 changed [basic.lookup.argdep]/4.2 to directly include all friends in the lookup", which agrees with my analysis. 
 I also found editorial issue #5302 against the draft standard, which presents a similar example. But this issue doesn't have a definitive outcome. 
 Lastly, I found CWG 143 , dated 1999. It says ADL works by finding "invisible" declarations in the namespace in which the associated classes are members, and not by finding friend declarations in associated classes (with an example similar to the one in this question). If the committee didn't change its mind, this means GCC's new behavior is incorrect.

 That clause is the trick. The abstract machine can retroactively create implicit-lifetime objects, choosing whatever set keeps your program defined. No constructor runs; the object just takes on the bytes already sitting there. Exactly what you want for bytes off a socket or malloc .

What are the differences between these two? 
 
 sched_setscheduler() is a system-call (wrapper), as we can know from the fact that it is documented in section 2 of the manual, if for no other reason. On Linux, the entities scheduled are native threads (not processes, contrary to another answer), identified by their native thread ids. These are the schedulable units. 
 pthread_setschedparam() is an ordinary-ish userspace function belonging to the Pthreads API. The entities scheduled are pthreads, which might or might not be tightly associated with native threads. When pthreads are associated with native threads, as in modern Glibc's pthreads implementation , this function relies on system interfaces such as sched_setscheduler() on the back end. It might or might not have additional pthreads-specific effects on the front end. It expects you to identify the subject (p)thread by its pthread ID. 
 Note well that, at least on Linux, native threads don't have to be created or managed via the Pthreads API. Whether a particular pthreads implementation creates or manages native threads at all is implementation-specific, though implementations that do so are overwhelmingly the norm these days. * On such implementations, all pthreads are closely associated with native threads, but particular native threads are not necessarily associated with pthreads. 
 
 Is there a compelling reason to use one over the other? 
 
 It is unspecified what metadata Pthreads maintains about the threads it manages, but there certainly is some. It follows that it is potentially unsafe to handle a pthreads-managed native thread via interfaces that don't account for Pthreads. And of course, on a system where Pthreads is not implemented on top of native threads, attempting to set scheduling parameters for an individual pthread via sched_setparams() will not have the intended effect. 
 And that may be why the Linux manual page for sched_setscheduler() says, in the VERSIONS section: 
 
 If you are using the POSIX threads API, then use pthread_setschedparam(3),
pthread_getschedparam(3), and pthread_setschedprio(3), instead of the sched_*(2) system calls. 
 
 I don't know whether you would consider that compelling , but it doesn't seem like you need to be compelled so much as advised: listen to the manual. If you're using pthreads, then do not bypass its interfaces to the scheduler.
